implementation_notes: The canonical dependency-free realization: a std::queue guarded by a std::mutex, with a std::condition_variable whose wait predicate is 'not empty' on the consumer side and 'not full' on the producer side; cppreference documents the required discipline (modify the guarded data under the lock, then notify, and re-check the predicate to survive spurious wakeups). notify_one hands each pushed item to exactly one waiting consumer, which is the point-to-point contract, and a stop flag plus notify_all ends the consumers at shutdown. Prefer it inside one process; reach for ZeroMQ only when the channel must span hosts.
pitfalls: Waking with notify_all on every push thundering-herds all consumers; notify_one plus a real queue keeps the hand-off one-to-one.
A consumer that exits while a predicate is not re-checked turns a spurious wakeup into a moved-from item.
Destruction order matters: consumers must join before the queue is destroyed, or a waiting thread touches freed memory.

variants.name: ZeroMQ PUSH/PULL pipeline
variants.idiom_name: zmq PUSH socket -> round-robin to PULL peers
variants.implementation_notes: libzmq ships the channel itself: a ZMQ_PUSH socket round-robins messages to all connected downstream nodes and a ZMQ_PULL socket fair-queues from all upstream nodes, so any number of workers may attach and each message is delivered to exactly one of them - the man page states messages are not discarded and sends block when every peer is at its high-water mark. Choose it when the channel must cross process or host boundaries and the application wants reconnection, load balancing and buffering handled by the socket type instead of a broker; it is not durable, so messages held in the socket die with the process.
pitfalls: ZMQ_PUSH round-robins blindly: unevenly fast workers cause head-of-line imbalance, and the mute state blocks the sender once all peers are full.
Sockets are not thread-safe except the newer thread-safe types; a PUSH socket shared across threads is undefined behaviour.
In-socket queues are in memory only - killing the process loses every buffered message, so durability needs a broker or store-and-forward.
